Q: Logbook 4 not logging trace-id for async response with Spring Boot 4 A:

Logbook itself does not propagate Micrometer trace context into its async logs. In Spring Boot 4+ the trace id/span id injection into MDC and async propagation is handled by Micrometer Tracing (Observations), not Logbook. Logbook 4 doesn’t automatically include async reactor trace ids in its own log lines.

Solution

  1. Ensure you have a proper Micrometer tracer implementation on the classpath, e.g.:

    implementation("org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-micrometer-tracing-brave")
implementation("io.micrometer:micrometer-tracing-bridge-brave")

    Or OpenTelemetry alternative. Without an actual tracer implementation Spring Boot won’t populate trace ids.

  2. Configure MDC/log pattern for trace id/span id so logs include them:

    logging:
  pattern:
    correlation: "[${spring.application.name:-},%X{traceId:-},%X{spanId:-}] "

    This makes Spring Boot emit correlation ids in logs.

  3. Propagate Reactor context into async work: Reactor execution loses thread‑local MDC/observation context unless propagated. Ensure automatic context propagation is enabled (e.g. Spring’s Reactor context propagation and use Hooks.enableAutomaticContextPropagation() if needed) so trace context travels through Mono chains.

  4. Logbook specific note: Logbook’s own request/response log entries are emitted outside of the reactive observation scope, so they won’t show trace info by default on async responses — this is a known limitation/behavior rather than a Spring Boot misconfig.

Summary:
Make sure Micrometer Tracing with a real tracer (Brave/OTel) is on the classpath, configure logging pattern to include %X{traceId}, and ensure Reactor context propagation so async execution retains trace context; Logbook itself won’t inject trace ids for async reactor responses without this context propagation

Q: What is the recommended learning roadmap for Hyperledger Fabric in 2026? A:

The Fabric documentation contains some getting started tutorials. The full stack asset transfer guide workshop material (in the samples repository) is also a good way to get going.

Having a basic understanding of Docker is useful since the sample test-network makes use of this. Docker is not essential for running Fabric though. The test-network-nano-bash demonstrates running a test network where each node is a local process instead of using Docker containers for each node.

For a production deployment, you probably want Kubernetes. Be aware of the Kubernetes builder to allow Fabric to start prebuilt chaincode imgages in Kubernetes pods as a preferred alternative to Fabric's default Docker-based chaincode builder.

Any of Go, TypeScript/JavaScript or Java are fully supported for writing smart contracts and client applications. If you have no preference between those languages, I would probably pick Go for smart contract implementation since that is the "reference" API implementation. For client applications, all three languages offer exactly equivalent support, so pick whichever suits your needs better.

Q: CodeLite building simple main issue A:

So, I have fighting with that for quite long time:

Go to settings. Click on Environment Variables. A window will open with default set. Just Add the line " SHELL = cmd.exe "

The fix is to add SHELL=cmd.exe to environment variables in CodeLite.

Q: is C++23 std::is_implicit_lifetime bugged today? A:

The definition of implicit-lifetime class is, from [class.prop]/8:

A class S is an implicit-lifetime class if

  • it is an aggregate whose destructor is not user-provided or
  • it has at least one trivial eligible constructor and a trivial, non-deleted destructor.

Your type is not an aggregate, so the first bullet does not apply.

But your type does have at least one trivial eligible constructor (both the move and copy constructor) and a trivial, non-deleted destructor, so the second bullet does apply.

Hence, it is implicit-lifetime.

Which, conceptually, makes sense. Since you can memcpy your type, it seems pretty meaningful to say that doing so (implicitly) starts the lifetime of an object at the place you copied it into.

Q: How to manually trigger Github Pull Request build A:

The issue is that your retrigger workflow calls the RTD API's versions endpoint to find an existing version for the PR - but if RTD never received the initial webhook, that version doesn't exist yet, so the query returns nothing.

Two approaches depending on your setup:

Option 1 - force RTD to register the PR via webhook re-delivery: Go to your GitHub repo Settings - Webhooks, find the RTD webhook, and look at Recent Deliveries. Find the pull_request event for that PR and click "Redeliver." This triggers the initial RTD registration without needing a new commit.

Option 2 - create the RTD version via API directly:

curl -X POST \
  -H "Authorization: Token YOUR_RTD_TOKEN" \
  https://readthedocs.org/api/v3/projects/{slug}/versions/ \
  -d '{"identifier": "refs/pull/{PR_NUMBER}/head"}'

This creates the external version manually, after which your existing retrigger workflow should work normally.

The root cause is usually a race condition where the PR opened before RTD's webhook was fully configured, or a transient webhook delivery failure.
